slope-from-points.why: Slope is the rate of change: how much the output moves per unit of input. It is the single most reused number in applied mathematics — speed, interest rate, cost per unit and the derivative are all slopes.
traps: Subtract the coordinates in the *same order* top and bottom. Reversing one gives the wrong sign.
A vertical line has an *undefined* slope, not a zero one. Zero slope is horizontal.

code.body:
def slope(p, q):
    return (q[1] - p[1]) / (q[0] - p[0])   # ZeroDivisionError if vertical
code.note: The *undefined* case is a real crash, not a theoretical nicety. Vertical lines are why slope-intercept form cannot describe every line.

slope-intercept.why: ~y = mx + b~ is the most useful form because both numbers you care about are visible: ~m~ is the rate and ~b~ is the starting value. Given it, you can sketch the line in seconds — plot ~b~ on the vertical axis, then step across and up by the slope.
traps: The sign belongs to the number: in ~y = 3x - 7~ the intercept is ~-7~.
The slope is the coefficient only when ~y~ is alone on one side. Rearrange first.

point-slope.why: Point-slope form exists because you usually know a rate and one observation, not the intercept. ~y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)~ lets you write the line immediately and convert later if you need to.
traps: Both minus signs are real: through ~(-2, 5)~ with slope 3 it is ~y - 5 = 3(x + 2)~.

standard-form.why: ~Ax + By = C~ treats ~x~ and ~y~ symmetrically, which makes both intercepts trivial — set each variable to zero in turn. It also handles vertical lines, which slope-intercept form cannot, and it is the form that systems of equations and linear programming use.
traps: Standard form hides the slope. If a question asks for the slope, rearrange rather than guessing from ~A~ and ~B~ — it is ~-A/B~.

parallel-perpendicular.why: Parallel lines share a slope. Perpendicular slopes multiply to ~-1~, which is the negative reciprocal: flip and change sign. The second fact is less obvious but it falls straight out of rotating a right triangle through ninety degrees.
traps: The negative reciprocal of ~\f{2}{3}~ is ~-\f{3}{2}~, not ~-\f{2}{3}~. Both operations are needed.
A horizontal line (slope 0) is perpendicular to a vertical one (*undefined* slope) — the product rule fails for that pair, which is the one exception.

linear-modelling.why: A linear model says a quantity starts somewhere and changes at a constant rate. Most real quantities are not exactly linear, but over a short enough stretch most of them are close enough — which is why this simple model earns its keep everywhere.
traps: Extrapolating far beyond your data is where linear models embarrass people. A straight line through a few points will happily predict negative populations.

line-of-best-fit.why: Real data never sits exactly on a line, so a line of best fit is the straight line that misses by the least overall. It gives you a slope you can interpret and a way to predict — but it is a summary of a pattern, not a law.
traps: A fitted slope shows association, not causation. The line cannot tell you which variable drives which, or whether a third thing drives both.
A high correlation can still hide a badly curved relationship. Look at the scatter, not only at ~r~.
